title: Human Factors in Patient Safety
path: Quality Improvement in Healthcare and Patient Safety

headings.title: Introduction to Human Factors and Ergonomics
headings.content: Human factors study the interrelationships between humans, tools, equipment, and the working environment in healthcare. Ergonomics applies this knowledge to optimize human well-being and overall system performance. Instead of blaming individuals when mistakes happen, human factors engineering examines why the system allowed the error to occur in the first place. Nurses interact constantly with monitors, infusion pumps, charts, and colleagues, making them central to ergonomic evaluations. Designing equipment that matches human physical and mental capabilities reduces stress and prevents adverse patient events.

headings.title: The Swiss Cheese Model of System Accidents
headings.content: James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model illustrates that patient harm rarely results from a single catastrophic failure. Instead, hazards pass through multiple defensive layers in an organization, each represented by a slice of Swiss cheese. The holes in the cheese represent latent conditions and active failures. Latent conditions include poor equipment design, understaffing, or inadequate training. Active failures are unsafe acts committed by frontline workers, such as skipping a double-check. An adverse event occurs only when the holes in every defensive layer momentarily align, creating a trajectory of accident opportunity.

headings.title: Cognitive Biases and Mental Workload in Nursing
headings.content:
Nurses process massive amounts of clinical data under intense time pressure, leading to high mental workload. When cognitive capacity is overloaded, shortcuts and cognitive biases emerge. 

- **Confirmation bias**: Searching for evidence that supports an initial impression while ignoring contradictory signs.
- **Anchoring**: Sticking stubbornly to the first diagnosis or impression, even when new vital signs suggest otherwise.
- **Availability heuristic**: Overestimating the likelihood of a complication simply because a similar case happened yesterday.

Recognizing these mental traps allows clinical teams to pause, review objective data, and perform structured safety checks.

headings.title: Physical Ergonomics and Environmental Design
headings.content: Physical ergonomics focuses on human anatomical, physiological, and biomechanical interactions with the workspace. In Nigerian hospitals, poor ward layouts, misplaced supply cupboards, and heavy manual patient lifting contribute heavily to nurse burnout and injuries. Ergonomic workspace design minimizes unnecessary bending, twisting, and walking distances. Standardized placement of emergency medications and supplies ensures that nurses can retrieve critical items quickly during resuscitation. Proper lighting, reduced ambient noise, and adjustable bed heights protect both staff musculoskeletal health and patient safety.

headings.title: Communication and Teamwork Human Factors
headings.content: Communication breakdowns remain a leading root cause of sentinel events in hospitals. Hierarchical structures often prevent junior nurses from speaking up when they notice a safety hazard. Standardized communication tools like **SBAR** (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) bridge this gap by providing a common language for handovers. Interprofessional briefing sessions build psychological safety, encouraging every team member to voice concerns regardless of rank. Clear closed-loop communication—where the receiver repeats an order back to the sender—prevents dangerous misunderstandings during medication administration.

headings.title: Fatigue, Stress, and Vigilance in Healthcare
headings.content: Extended work shifts, high nurse-to-patient ratios, and night duties induce severe physical and mental fatigue. Chronic fatigue impairs sustained attention, slows reaction times, and degrades working memory. Vigilance decrement occurs when a nurse's ability to monitor continuous displays or subtle patient changes drops over time. Recognizing fatigue as a system hazard rather than a personal weakness is crucial. Implementing safe rostering practices, adequate break times, and peer-monitoring systems helps protect patients from fatigue-related lapses.

headings.title: Designing Systems to Prevent Human Error
headings.content: System design should anticipate human fallibility and build defensive mechanisms into everyday tasks. **Forcing functions** make it impossible to perform an action incorrectly, such as plugs that only fit into specific sockets. **Standardization** reduces cognitive load by keeping equipment layouts and procedures identical across units. **Redundancy**, like double-checking high-risk chemotherapy calculations with a colleague, catches errors before they reach the patient. Creating fail-safe workflows protects both vulnerable patients and well-meaning clinical staff.

headings.title: Applying Human Factors in Nigerian Clinical Settings
headings.content: Applying human factors principles in Nigerian healthcare requires navigating unique challenges such as erratic power supply, resource scarcity, and heavy workloads. When equipment fails or consumables run short, nurses often resort to improvising, which introduces workaround risks. Cultivating a **just culture** is essential—a environment where staff feel safe reporting errors and near-misses without fear of punitive victimization. By focusing on root-cause analysis during adverse event reviews rather than assigning blame, Nigerian health institutions can systematically redesign safer clinical workflows.
